raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old man presented with pain in his lower limbs and non-itchy, erythematous rash over both lower limbs. He had low-grade intermittent fever of three-months duration. On examination, the patient was pale and had palpable purpura over both thighs and buttocks [Figure 1]. He was malnourished (body mass index = 18.4 kg/m2), and abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly.
A complete blood count suggested pancytopenia (hemoglobin = 6.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count = 2800/mm3, and thrombocyte count = 45 000/muL). Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL) was noted with normal liver and renal function tests. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen confirmed hepatosplenomegaly and was otherwise unremarkable.
We considered hematological malignancy or a connective tissue disorder with vasculitis. Other infectious etiologies entertained were HIV, scrub typhus rickettsia, and visceral leishmaniasis (given the patient lived in an endemic area). Anti-nuclear antibodies, complement levels (C3 = 94 mg/dL and C4 = 20 mg/dL), and rheumatoid factor were negative. Urine examination was normal and serum cryoglobulins were not raised. Viral markers (HIV, hepatitis B surface antigen, and anti-hepatitis C) were negative. Serology for rickettsia and scrub typhus were also negative. Peripheral blood antibodies towards rK39 antigen were positive, and bone marrow examination confirmed visceral leishmaniasis with the presence of typical Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigote form) within the bone marrow histiocytes [Figure 2]. Skin biopsy of the rashes revealed fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall along with extravasation of red blood cells and nuclear debris in the adjoining areas consistent with a diagnosis of leukocytoclastic vasculitis [Figure 3].
Conventional amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) was given for 14 days with close monitoring of electrolytes, renal function, and urine output along with adequate nutritional support. During treatment, the patient's fever resolved, his blood counts improved, and we noted complete resolution of skin rash.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old male presented with lower limb pain, a non-pruritic erythematous rash over both lower limbs, and intermittent low-grade fever for three months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-month history of low-grade intermittent fever, bilateral lower extremity pain, and non-itchy erythematous skin eruptions across both lower extremities. Because of worsening symptoms and development of palpable purpura, he was admitted for evaluation of suspected vasculitis, systemic hematological disease, or chronic occult infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in an endemic area for visceral leishmaniasis. No prior chronic medical illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pain in bilateral lower limbs; non-itchy rash. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General appearance: pale, malnourished with a body mass index (BMI) of 18.4 kg/m2. Dermatologic: palpable purpura over bilateral thighs and buttocks. Abdomen: palpable hepatomegaly with massive splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin: 6.8 g/dL; Total leukocyte count: 2,800/mm3; Platelet count: 45,000/muL (pancytopenia). Serum globulins: polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (4.9 g/dL). Liver and renal function tests: normal. Urinalysis: normal. Complement levels: C3 94 mg/dL, C4 20 mg/dL. Autoimmune serologies: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) negative; serum cryoglobulins not elevated. Infectious serologies: HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, scrub typhus, and rickettsial serology all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of chest and abdomen: confirmed hepatosplenomegaly, otherwise unremarkable. Skin biopsy of purpuric rash: fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls with extravasation of red blood cells and nuclear debris in adjoining areas, consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis. Bone marrow examination: bone marrow biopsy and aspiration performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis complicated by secondary leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood rK39 antigen antibodies were positive; bone marrow examination demonstrated typical Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies (amastigote form) within bone marrow histiocytes.
Differentials ruled out: Primary systemic vasculitis / connective tissue disorders (negative ANA, RF, cryoglobulins, normal C3 and C4), hematologic malignancy, HIV, viral hepatitis B and C, scrub typhus, and rickettsial infections.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with conventional intravenous amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg/day) for 14 days with intensive monitoring of electrolytes, renal function, and urine output, alongside nutritional support. Achieved resolution of fever, recovery of blood cell counts, and complete disappearance of palpable purpura.
